summary.text: A 24-year-old male boxing instructor presented to an orthopedic clinic with recurrent dislocation of both shoulders. The first left anterior dislocation occurred five years earlier in a football match, followed a few months later by a right anterior dislocation. Recurrent episodes during physical activity brought severe pain, loss of function and instability despite immobilization and physiotherapy.

Examination showed bilateral shoulder laxity with positive apprehension, relocation and anterior drawer tests, limited range of motion and a normal neurovascular examination. Radiographs and CT showed bilateral glenoid bone loss of less than 20% with Hill-Sachs lesions, and MRI showed anterior labral tears, Bankart lesions and soft tissue injuries. Bilateral recurrent shoulder dislocation with glenoid bone loss and Hill-Sachs lesions was diagnosed.

After discussing options, risks and benefits and giving informed consent, the patient had an open Latarjet procedure on the left shoulder first and on the right shoulder one month later, under general anesthesia. Coracoid autograft blocks were screwed to the anterior glenoid rim through a deltopectoral approach, with labral repair and capsular plication. Postoperative radiographs were satisfactory and a structured rehabilitation program with regular follow-up followed.

At the one-year follow-up the patient showed substantial improvement in both shoulders, with no reported recurrence of dislocation or instability and a return to work as a boxing instructor and to activities without restriction. Forward flexion and abduction reached full range of motion and external rotation was nearly full. He was satisfied and remains in outpatient follow-up.

article_limitations: Visual status of figures in this annotation stays not_inspected; actual pixels are reviewed in visual.json.
The case gives no calendar dates; the right-sided operation is "one month later" than the left and the one-year follow-up is not anchored to either operation.

Figures 1 to 3 captions locate the CT and MRI findings in the right shoulder while the text findings are bilateral; the caption findings are kept as separate right-shoulder observations. Figure 4 to 6 captions do not state the operated side.
The Figure 13 caption gives about 60-70 degrees external rotation while the text says nearly full; kept as separate facts, not merged.
The Figure 9 caption calls the radiograph a scapular Y view while the image prints "AP"; the caption fact is review_only and the projection is not resolved.
Discussion paragraphs describe literature and general recommendations; only sentences that literally say "in our case" or "the patient" are attributed to the index patient.
The patient positioning sentence (supine, propped up 30 degrees, sandbag under the right shoulder) is not recorded as a separate fact; it is not tied to either side of surgery.
